title: Isaiah (Part 3)
hook: God could have simply forgiven and moved on, but instead He commands the heavens themselves to comfort His people—doubling the word, as if once were not enough to convey the urgency: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people." That single Hebrew repetition carries the weight of an exile's worth of grief, and it opens onto some of the most breathtaking chapters in all of scripture, where God puts the nations on trial, calls a pagan Persian king His "anointed," and asks Israel a question that still lands like a blow: "Have ye not known? have ye not heard?" This is not abstract theology. It's the record of a God who names His people, claims them as His own creation, and refuses to let their failure be the final word—even when that people had every reason to believe otherwise. Isaiah 40–49 moves from courtroom to comfort to covenant renewal so fluidly that it's easy to miss how radical each turn really is: judgment gives way to tenderness, and tenderness gives way to purpose. Come see how the same God who silences nations also bends down to console the brokenhearted—and ask yourself what it means to be called by His name.
